screens.title: Shared Responsibility Model & IAM Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we will make two foundational ideas clear and practical. First, the Shared Responsibility Model: AWS secures the underlying cloud infrastructure — the physical datacenters, hypervisors, and global network — while you as the customer secure everything you run inside that cloud, including your data, operating systems, configurations, applications, and identity controls. I will show concrete examples so that this boundary is never ambiguous. Second, Identity and Access Management, or IAM, is the system you use to control who can do what in your account. You will learn the four core IAM entities — users, groups, roles, and policies — and the recommended patterns such as using roles for temporary credentials and enforcing the principle of least privilege. We will also cover Multi-Factor Authentication and how it defends accounts even when a password is stolen. By the end, you will know which responsibilities are handled by AWS, which are yours, and practical steps to create a user, group, attach a read-only policy, and enable MFA. Keep in mind a common misconception: thinking AWS covers your data and OS patching. It does not. That distinction is the first defense for robust, compliant security.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Overview

Shared Responsibility Model & IAM Fundamentals

Understand which security responsibilities belong to AWS and which belong to you, plus how IAM enforces access control.

In this lesson

Why it matters

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next lesson segments you will learn four practical competencies. First, you will explain the Shared Responsibility Model and map specific responsibilities to AWS or the customer, so you can avoid common security gaps. Second, you will identify IAM core components — users, groups, roles, and policies — and describe their relationships so you can design correct access models. Third, you will apply the principle of least privilege when drafting IAM policies, with a concrete habit of granting only needed actions on a single resource. Fourth, you will configure Multi-Factor Authentication for the root account and for IAM users to protect high-privilege logins. Each objective has an explicit milestone you can verify: explain the model with examples, list IAM entities and their use cases, show a least-privilege policy for a real task, and demonstrate MFA enrollment. These skills matter because misapplied responsibility boundaries or overly broad permissions are common causes of breaches. I will give examples that map to realistic scenarios, such as patching an EC2 instance versus securing the hypervisor, and designing an EC2 role to read from a single S3 bucket. By the end you will have repeatable steps to secure identities and a checklist to avoid typical mistakes.

screens.title: Understanding the Shared Responsibility Model
screens.narratorSegment: The Shared Responsibility Model draws a clear line: AWS is responsible for the security of the cloud, and you are responsible for security in the cloud. Saying it another way, AWS protects the physical facilities, hardware, network, and foundational services such as the hypervisor and managed database engines. Your responsibilities cover everything you deploy: your data, operating systems, application code, identity configuration, encryption keys you control, and network configuration inside your virtual networks. A concrete example: AWS ensures EC2's hypervisor is maintained and patched; you must patch the operating system on the EC2 instance you run. Another example: AWS provides the S3 service and underlying storage durability; you must configure bucket permissions and encrypt sensitive objects. A common misconception is to assume AWS's responsibility includes configuration mistakes you make—this is false. If a developer leaves an S3 bucket open to the public, that is a customer responsibility. Why that matters: most security incidents in cloud environments involve misconfigured services or over-permissive identity policies under customer control. To check your understanding, ask whether the issue arises from physical infrastructure or from how you configured a resource. If it’s the latter, it’s your responsibility to fix it. This mental model steers operational tasks, compliance scopes, and incident response plans.

keyIdea.title: Defining the boundary
keyIdea.text: AWS secures infrastructure and services; customers secure data, configurations, and access inside their accounts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Shared Responsibility
Definition

Security of the cloud vs Security in the cloud

The responsibility boundary separates AWS-managed infrastructure from customer-managed resources and configurations. Keep this separation clear for operational security and compliance.

AWS is responsible for:
Physical datacenters, hardware, hypervisor, managed service control planes, and global network security.
You are responsible for:
Your data, OS patching, network configuration, IAM, application-level controls, and client-side encryption.
Key Takeaway

Treat AWS as the infrastructure provider; treat your team as the operator of everything you deploy. Misconfigurations remain customer liability.

Examples & Misconceptions
Example: EC2
AWS secures the hypervisor and physical host. You patch and harden the guest OS and control inbound firewall rules.
Example: S3
AWS maintains storage durability. You configure bucket policies, ACLs, and object encryption to protect your data.
Common mistake
Assuming AWS configures your resources securely by default; in fact, customer configuration sets many outcomes.
Why it matters
Responsible partitioning clarifies incident response and compliance responsibilities.
Reflective question
If an S3 object is leaked, was it a service failure or a configuration issue? How would you prove it?

screens.title: AWS Responsibilities — "Security of the cloud"
screens.narratorSegment: When we say AWS covers the security of the cloud, we mean the physical and foundational layers of the service stack. AWS maintains datacenter facilities, physical access controls, host hardware, the virtualization layer including the hypervisor, and managed control planes for services such as S3, RDS, and the networking backbone. This reduces your operational burden because AWS takes care of patching, availability, and large-scale infrastructure integrity. For example, AWS ensures that the EC2 hypervisor receives security updates and that the network fabric is resilient. It also manages certain service control planes so you never manually operate the storage backend for S3. A common misconception is expecting AWS to manage application-level configuration or tenant data; they do not. Understanding exactly which layers AWS protects lets you focus your team on the remaining responsibilities: identity controls, host-level security, encryption, and correct service configuration. When designing architectures, assume AWS will handle hardware and service availability, and design your monitoring, encryption, and access controls around the layers you own. A design checklist item: confirm whether a risk maps to infrastructure or deployed resources; if it maps to deployed resources, your team must mitigate it.

keyIdea.title: AWS-managed layers
keyIdea.text: AWS secures physical datacenters, hardware, hypervisors, and managed service control planes — allowing you to focus on application and data controls.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › AWS Responsibilities
Architecture View

Infrastructure and control planes

AWS is responsible for physical facilities, host hardware, hypervisors, managed service control planes, and the global network fabric. These responsibilities support durability and availability for customers.
Physical datacenters
Redundant facilities, physical access control, and environmental protection.
Virtualization layer
Hypervisor maintenance and isolation between tenants.
Managed services
Control planes for services such as S3 and RDS operate under AWS responsibility.
Practical implications
Operational benefit
Less effort on hardware patching; focus ops on configuration, encryption, and identity.
Design checklist
When auditing risk, confirm whether it maps to infrastructure (AWS) or customer resources (you). If customer, plan remediation.
Misconception
Assuming managed services cover your data access policies; they do not. You must configure access controls and encryption.

screens.title: Customer Responsibilities — "Security in the cloud"
screens.narratorSegment: Security in the cloud is everything you and your team must actively manage. This includes your data, the operating systems on virtual machines, application-level controls, network configuration such as security groups and firewalls, identity and access management settings, and encryption keys you manage or control access to. A practical example: if you launch an EC2 instance, you are responsible for applying OS patches, configuring host-based firewalls, and ensuring that any credentials on that host are rotated and stored securely. Another example: for S3, you must set bucket policies, object ACLs, and encryption options; AWS provides the storage service but not your permissions choices. A common mistake is relying on default console settings without reviewing permissions. Default configurations may be permissive in ways that are convenient for initial testing but unsafe in production. To operate securely, adopt clear processes: use IAM roles instead of embedding long-lived access keys, restrict A P I actions with narrow policies, enforce encryption at rest and in transit, and keep a patching cadence for any guest operating systems. The practical payoff is preventing avoidable exposures and making incident response straightforward because responsibilities were assigned and executed.

keyIdea.title: Customer-managed areas
keyIdea.text: You must secure data, operating systems, identity configurations, network rules, and encryption for resources you deploy.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Customer Responsibilities
Scope

What you must secure

Data and object permissions — you control access and encryption choices.
Operating systems and application patching on guest instances.
Network configuration such as security group rules and NACLs.
Identity and Access Management: who can act, and with what permissions.
Practical rule

Use roles for service access, rotate credentials, enable logging, and enforce encryption to minimize exposure from misconfiguration.

Example
You launch an EC2 instance: AWS secures the host; you secure the OS patching, SSH keys, and the IAM role or credentials used by applications on the instance.
Gotcha
Leaving test or default permissions in production is still a customer responsibility and a frequent source of incidents.

screens.title: IAM Overview — Users, Groups, Roles, Policies
screens.narratorSegment: IAM is the central service for authentication and authorization in AWS. It uses four core entity types. First, an IAM User represents a person or application with long-lived credentials such as a console password or access keys. Users are suitable for individuals who need stable identities. Second, an IAM Group is a collection of users; groups simplify management by letting you attach policies once and have every member inherit them. Third, an IAM Role is an identity that can be assumed by trusted entities — another AWS service, an EC2 instance, a Lambda function, or a user from another account — and it provides temporary credentials while assumed. Roles are preferred for services and temporary access because they avoid embedding static keys. Fourth, IAM Policies are JSON documents that explicitly allow or deny actions on resources; you attach policies to users, groups, or roles. A concrete example: create a group named S3ReadOnlyGroup with the AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess policy, add a user to that group, and the user can list and view objects but cannot create buckets. A common misconception is treating roles and users as interchangeable; they are not. Roles do not have long-lived credentials and are safer for services. Reflect: when would a role reduce risk compared to distributing access keys?

keyIdea.title: IAM building blocks
keyIdea.text: Users, groups, roles, and policies combine to express who can do what, where, and for how long.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › IAM Overview
Entities
IAM User — person or application with credentials for console or API access.
IAM Group — collection of users; attach policies to groups to simplify management.
IAM Role — assumable identity that provides temporary credentials to services or users.
IAM Policy — JSON document that allows or denies actions on resources; attachable to users, groups, or roles.
Concrete scenario
Scenario: EC2 needs to read from one S3 bucket. Best practice: attach an instance role with a policy granting s3:GetObject on that bucket instead of placing access keys on the instance.
Misconception
Do not use IAM users with embedded keys for services; roles are safer and intended for that purpose.
Key Takeaway

Match entity type to use case: users for people, groups for management, roles for services and temporary access, policies to define permissions.

screens.title: Creating an IAM Group and User (Lab Walkthrough)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the lab steps you will perform to create a group, a user, and attach S3 read-only permissions. Step one: create an IAM group named S3ReadOnlyGroup and attach the AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess managed policy. This gives the group the correct scope of actions for listing and reading objects. Step two: create an IAM user named s3-reader-user with both console and programmatic access. Assign the user to the group and download the CSV containing the access key and secret if programmatic testing is needed. Step three: test console access by opening an incognito browser and signing in with the user's console URL and the password you set — you should be able to list buckets and view objects but not create new buckets or upload objects. Step four: configure a named AWS CLI profile with the downloaded keys and run the AWS CLI list command to confirm list access. A common error is not placing the user in the group; if so, the user will be denied. Another common error is leaving long-lived keys where they can be accessed by applications; prefer roles for EC2 and other services. After the tests, remove any credentials used for the lab.

keyIdea.title: Lab flow
keyIdea.text: Create group, create user, attach policy, verify console and CLI behavior, and clean up credentials after testing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Lab Walkthrough
Steps
  1. Create IAM group S3ReadOnlyGroup and attach AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess.
  2. Create IAM user s3-reader-user with console and programmatic access.
  3. Add the user to the S3ReadOnlyGroup and download the access key CSV.
  4. Verify console sign-in and test listing buckets; confirm create bucket fails.
  5. Optional: configure AWS CLI profile and run aws s3 ls to confirm programmatic access.
Common mistake
Forgetting to add the user to the group or attaching overly broad policies instead of the least-privilege managed policy.
Terminal-style snippets
# Configure CLI profile for s3-reader-user
aws configure --profile s3-reader-user
# Then list buckets with that profile
aws s3 ls --profile s3-reader-user
Expected: listing succeeds; creating a bucket should return Access Denied for this read-only role.

screens.title: IAM Roles and Temporary Credentials
screens.narratorSegment: IAM Roles grant permissions that trusted entities can assume and receive temporary credentials. Unlike IAM users, roles do not have long-lived access keys attached; instead, when an entity assumes a role it receives short-lived credentials that expire automatically. This is particularly important for services that need access, such as EC2 instances or Lambda functions. A practical example: an EC2 instance that needs to read objects from an S3 bucket should assume an instance profile role with s3:GetObject permissions, rather than storing an access key on the instance. This eliminates the risk of leaked long-lived keys. Another example is cross-account access: a role can be assumed by a principal in another AWS account with explicit trust. A frequent misconception is to assume rotating long-lived keys is equivalent to using roles; rotating keys reduces risk but still leaves windows of exposure. Temporary credentials reduce that window dramatically and simplify credential management. When you design access for services, prefer roles. Ask yourself: if credentials were exposed, how long would they remain valid? If the answer is more than a few minutes, prefer temporary credentials via roles.

keyIdea.title: Roles vs Users
keyIdea.text: Roles provide temporary, assumable credentials that reduce the risk associated with long-lived keys and are ideal for services and cross-account access.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Roles & Temporary Credentials
How roles work
A role defines permissions and a trust policy. When assumed, it issues temporary credentials that expire. Roles are attached to compute resources like EC2 via instance profiles, or assumed by services and users.
Example
EC2 instance with an instance profile that grants s3:GetObject on a specific bucket; the instance uses temporary credentials provided by the role.
Design guidance
  • Prefer roles for services and cross-account access.
  • Avoid storing long-lived keys on instances or in code repositories.
  • Use trust policies to restrict who can assume a role.
Misconception
Rotating long-lived keys is useful, but roles with short-lived credentials provide stronger protection by default.

screens.title: IAM Policies — Structure and a Simple Example
screens.narratorSegment: IAM Policies are JSON documents that state allowed or denied actions on resources. They bind identity (user, group, or role) to permissions. The simplest and safest approach is to scope a policy to precise actions and a narrow resource. For example, grant only s3:GetObject on a specific bucket and path. That prevents broader S3 actions like bucket creation or deletion. I'll describe one concrete policy: it allows the s3:GetObject action on the resource arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/* and denies nothing else, so the principal can only fetch objects from that bucket. A common mistake is using wildcards like s3:* or resource "*", which grants too-wide privileges. Another error is attaching the wrong policy level; attaching a permissive policy to a group grants it to all members. After you write a policy, test it with a user or role and observe expected Allow and Deny behavior. When you design policies, follow least privilege: start narrow, test, and expand only when necessary. How would you adjust the example if the application also needed to list bucket contents? You would add s3:ListBucket with resource limited to the bucket ARN and include condition keys if needed.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › IAM Policy Example
Policy structure
Policies include Version, Statement, Effect, Action, Resource, and optional Conditions. Keep statements focused and resource ARNs specific.
Concrete example policy
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/*"
    }
  ]
}
Explanation & pitfalls
  • Effect: Allow or Deny. Use Deny sparingly to override complex allow rules.
  • Action: list specific API actions rather than broad categories when possible.
  • Resource: scope to the exact ARN, not "*", to limit blast radius.
Common mistake
Using s3:* or resource "*" grants excessive permissions and violates least privilege.

screens.title: Principle of Least Privilege
screens.narratorSegment: The principle of least privilege states you should grant the minimal set of permissions needed to perform a task. This is not just abstract security advice — it materially reduces the impact of compromised credentials or misconfigurations. Consider an app that needs to read from a single S3 bucket. The least-privilege policy grants s3:GetObject on that bucket only. The less secure alternative would grant s3:* on all buckets. If the credentials are leaked, the least-privilege approach limits the attacker to reading a narrow data set, while the broad approach exposes all buckets. A practical way to apply the principle is to start with deny-all, then add explicit allows for required actions and resources, or start with a very narrow allow and expand only when your application errors show missing permissions. A common operational mistake is granting broad permissions for convenience during development and forgetting to tighten them before production. Make least privilege part of your deployment checklist: review policies, use groups to centralize permissions, and use roles for services. Reflect: when was a permission added for convenience that you can now remove or scope down?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Least Privilege
Comparison
Least-privilege example
Allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/* only.
Over-privileged example
Allow s3:* on resource "*" — grants excessive control and increases risk.
Practical steps
  1. Identify the exact actions an application needs.
  2. Create a policy that grants only those actions on specific ARNs.
  3. Attach the policy to a role for services or a group for users.
  4. Periodically review and tighten policies based on actual use.
Key Takeaway

Least privilege limits blast radius and is a continuous practice: design narrow, verify, and prune permissions over time.

screens.title: Configuring Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
screens.narratorSegment: Multi-Factor Authentication adds a second factor to sign-in, combining something you know with something you have. Enabling MFA for the root account and for high-privilege IAM users is strongly recommended because it makes credential theft far less effective. Typical MFA types include virtual MFA devices on a phone, hardware security keys, and dedicated hardware tokens. A simple flow to enable virtual MFA for an IAM user: sign in to the AWS console as that user or an administrator, navigate to the user's security credentials, choose to assign a virtual MFA device, scan the QR code with an authenticator app, and enter two successive time-based codes to confirm alignment. A common misconception is that MFA is optional for non-admins; in many environments, enforcing MFA for administrative groups is a compliance requirement and an important defense. For programmatic access, MFA can be combined with temporary session tokens where required. After enabling MFA, test console sign-in and confirm that access requires the one-time code in addition to the password. Consider enforcing MFA with an IAM policy that denies console access unless aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true for sensitive groups. How would you enforce this for an Admins group? Attach a policy denying console actions unless MFA is present.

keyIdea.text: Enable virtual MFA for root and admin users and enforce MFA via policy for critical accounts to reduce the risk of credential compromise.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Multi-Factor Authentication
Steps to enable virtual MFA
  1. Sign in with the user or admin account and open the IAM console.
  2. Choose the user, open Security credentials, and select Manage MFA device.
  3. Select Virtual MFA device, scan the QR code with an authenticator app, and enter two consecutive codes to confirm.
  4. Test console sign-in to confirm the one-time code is required.
Tip
Enable MFA for the root account immediately after creation and require MFA for Admin groups via policy.
Enforcing MFA with policy
Attach a policy to deny console access unless aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true. This automates enforcement across a group of users and ensures compliance with administrative requirements.
Misconception
MFA is not a replacement for good policies; it is an additional protective layer that should be combined with least privilege and monitoring.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Operational Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Security misconfigurations often stem from common operational mistakes. The first frequent error is using long-lived access keys for services instead of roles. This creates a persistent credential that can be leaked. The second mistake is granting overly broad permissions during development and forgetting to tighten them before production. Wildcard actions or resource "*" are typical culprits. Third, failing to enable MFA for root and administrative accounts leaves high-privilege logins vulnerable. Fourth, not regularly reviewing attached policies and group membership allows privilege creep over time. To avoid these mistakes, adopt a checklist: prefer roles for service access, grant least privilege with narrow policies, enable and enforce MFA, and perform periodic reviews of policies and access logs. Include automation where possible: use IAM Access Analyzer or policy scanning to detect broad grants, and integrate policy checks into your deployment pipeline. A practical habit is to require peer review for policy changes and restrict who can attach policies in the first place. Finally, if an incident occurs, use the Shared Responsibility Model to quickly determine whether the root cause was an AWS infrastructure component or a customer configuration, so you can respond appropriately.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Mistakes & Best Practices
Common mistakes
  • Storing long-lived access keys on instances or in code repositories.
  • Using wildcard actions or resource "*" in policies for convenience.
  • Not enabling MFA for root and administrative users.
  • Neglecting periodic policy and membership reviews, causing privilege creep.
Operational checklist
Use roles for services and temporary credentials to minimize key exposure.
Enforce least privilege and require policy reviews for changes.
Enable MFA and optionally enforce it with IAM policies for admin groups.
Automate scans for overbroad policies and integrate checks into CI/CD.

Welcome. In this lesson we will make two foundational ideas clear and practical. First, the Shared Responsibility Model: AWS secures the underlying cloud infrastructure — the physical datacenters, hypervisors, and global network — while you as the customer secure everything you run inside that cloud, including your data, operating systems, configurations, applications, and identity controls. I will show concrete examples so that this boundary is never ambiguous. Second, Identity and Access Management, or IAM, is the system you use to control who can do what in your account. You will learn the four core IAM entities — users, groups, roles, and policies — and the recommended patterns such as using roles for temporary credentials and enforcing the principle of least privilege. We will also cover Multi-Factor Authentication and how it defends accounts even when a password is stolen. By the end, you will know which responsibilities are handled by AWS, which are yours, and practical steps to create a user, group, attach a read-only policy, and enable MFA. Keep in mind a common misconception: thinking AWS covers your data and OS patching. It does not. That distinction is the first defense for robust, compliant security.

Over the next lesson segments you will learn four practical competencies. First, you will explain the Shared Responsibility Model and map specific responsibilities to AWS or the customer, so you can avoid common security gaps. Second, you will identify IAM core components — users, groups, roles, and policies — and describe their relationships so you can design correct access models. Third, you will apply the principle of least privilege when drafting IAM policies, with a concrete habit of granting only needed actions on a single resource. Fourth, you will configure Multi-Factor Authentication for the root account and for IAM users to protect high-privilege logins. Each objective has an explicit milestone you can verify: explain the model with examples, list IAM entities and their use cases, show a least-privilege policy for a real task, and demonstrate MFA enrollment. These skills matter because misapplied responsibility boundaries or overly broad permissions are common causes of breaches. I will give examples that map to realistic scenarios, such as patching an EC2 instance versus securing the hypervisor, and designing an EC2 role to read from a single S3 bucket. By the end you will have repeatable steps to secure identities and a checklist to avoid typical mistakes.

This screen sets practical lab outcomes you will prove during the hands-on activity. You will create an IAM group and an IAM user, attach the AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess policy to the group, and verify that the user can list S3 buckets but cannot create a bucket. You will also download and configure programmatic credentials and test them with the AWS command line, observing expected "Access Denied" behavior for disallowed actions. A final practice is enabling a virtual MFA device for the newly created user and confirming console sign-in requires the MFA code. These outcomes teach concrete verification: creating and assigning permissions, confirming least-privilege behavior, and enforcing MFA. This matters because theory without verification leaves gaps; the lab proves the model works and reveals likely misconfigurations, such as attaching overly broad permissions or failing to require MFA for privileged accounts. As you practice, note the verification points: group policy attachment, console behavior, CLI behavior, and MFA enforcement. These checks are repeatable and map directly to real operational controls you will use in production environments.

The Shared Responsibility Model draws a clear line: AWS is responsible for the security of the cloud, and you are responsible for security in the cloud. Saying it another way, AWS protects the physical facilities, hardware, network, and foundational services such as the hypervisor and managed database engines. Your responsibilities cover everything you deploy: your data, operating systems, application code, identity configuration, encryption keys you control, and network configuration inside your virtual networks. A concrete example: AWS ensures EC2's hypervisor is maintained and patched; you must patch the operating system on the EC2 instance you run. Another example: AWS provides the S3 service and underlying storage durability; you must configure bucket permissions and encrypt sensitive objects. A common misconception is to assume AWS's responsibility includes configuration mistakes you make—this is false. If a developer leaves an S3 bucket open to the public, that is a customer responsibility. Why that matters: most security incidents in cloud environments involve misconfigured services or over-permissive identity policies under customer control. To check your understanding, ask whether the issue arises from physical infrastructure or from how you configured a resource. If it’s the latter, it’s your responsibility to fix it. This mental model steers operational tasks, compliance scopes, and incident response plans.

AWS maintains datacenter facilities, physical access controls, host hardware, the virtualization layer including the hypervisor, and managed control planes for services such as S3, RDS, and the networking backbone. This reduces your operational burden because AWS takes care of patching, availability, and large-scale infrastructure integrity. For example, AWS ensures that the EC2 hypervisor receives security updates and that the network fabric is resilient. It also manages certain service control planes so you never manually operate the storage backend for S3. A common misconception is expecting AWS to manage application-level configuration or tenant data; they do not. A design checklist item: confirm whether a risk maps to infrastructure or deployed resources; if it maps to deployed resources, your team must mitigate it.

Security in the cloud is everything you and your team must actively manage. This includes your data, the operating systems on virtual machines, application-level controls, network configuration such as security groups and firewalls, identity and access management settings, and encryption keys you manage or control access to. The practical payoff is preventing avoidable exposures and making incident response straightforward because responsibilities were assigned and executed.

IAM is the central service for authentication and authorization in AWS. It uses four core entity types. Reflect: when would a role reduce risk compared to distributing access keys?
